evals.name: portfolio-allocation-ira-rollover
evals.prompt: I'm 42, married, and just rolled over an old 401(k) into an IRA with about $85k in it. I won't touch it until retirement (~25 years). I'd call myself middle-of-the-road on risk. How should I split this across funds?
evals.expected_output: Applies the age/risk allocation formulas: middle-of-the-road at 42 -> bonds = 42-10 = 32%, stocks = 110-42 = 68%; ~1/3 of stocks overseas (~23% intl, ~45% US). Shows the arithmetic, recommends low-cost index funds, notes it's a retirement account (so tax placement is moot / chase yield), keeps fund count small. Educational-not-licensed caveat.
assertions: Computes the bond allocation as ~32% using age-10 (42-10)
Computes the stock allocation as ~68% using 110-age (110-42)
Recommends putting roughly one-third of the stock sleeve in international funds
Recommends low-cost index funds
Notes that inside an IRA taxes are sheltered, so tax-placement/tax-free-fund concerns don't apply
Shows the allocation arithmetic explicitly rather than just stating percentages
Includes an educational / not-a-licensed-advisor style caveat

evals.name: screen-load-fund
evals.prompt: My broker is recommending the American Funds Growth Fund of America Class A shares — 5.75% up front, 0.64% expense ratio. Is this a good deal or should I look elsewhere?
evals.expected_output: Flags the 5.75% front-end load as the dominant problem (a commission paid out of invested money that buys nothing), recommends no-load alternatives, notes Class A = front-end load share class, applies cost-first screening. May note the 0.64% expense ratio isn't terrible but the load is disqualifying. Debunks broker myths. Educational caveat.
assertions: Identifies the 5.75% up-front charge as a front-end load / sales commission
Recommends avoiding the load and considering no-load alternatives
Explains that a load buys nothing in fund quality (goes to the broker, not management)
Treats the 0.64% expense ratio as secondary to the load (not itself disqualifying)
Correctly labels Class A shares as the front-end-load share class
Includes an educational / not-a-licensed-advisor style caveat

evals.name: beginner-debt-first-foundation
evals.prompt: I'm 28, have about $6k in credit card debt at 19% APR, no emergency fund, but I really want to start investing in index funds. Where do I begin, and how do I keep taxes low?
evals.expected_output: Enforces foundation-first: pay off the 19% credit card debt before investing (can't out-earn 19% with ~8-9% returns), build a 3-6 month emergency reserve in a money market fund, capture any employer 401(k) match, THEN invest in low-cost index funds. Addresses tax question (tax-advantaged accounts first; index funds are tax-efficient). Does not just hand over a fund allocation. Educational caveat.
assertions: Advises paying off the 19% credit card debt before investing in funds
Explains you can't reliably out-earn 19% interest with ~8-9% investment returns
Recommends building a 3-6 month emergency reserve, ideally in a money market fund
Mentions capturing an employer 401(k) match / using tax-advantaged accounts first
Does NOT lead with a stock/bond fund allocation as the primary answer (foundation first)
Recommends low-cost index funds once the foundation is in place
Includes an educational / not-a-licensed-advisor style caveat
